result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.alt_heuristic()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Build an ALT landmark heuristic for A\* search. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.alt_heuristic()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Build an ALT landmark heuristic for A\* search. title: >- [Graph.alt_heuristic()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Build an ALT landmark heuristic for A\* search. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Build an ALT landmark heuristic for A* search. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L53653-L53781){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.alt_heuristic( k=8, method="farthest", landmarks=None, seed=None, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![ALT heuristic](../assets/graphs/alt-heuristic.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-by-six grid with the four landmarks chosen by farthest-point selection filled in teal: (4,0), (0,5), (5,4) and (0,0), the last also the source. Each node is labeled with the ALT bound h on its distance to the target (5,5), outlined; on this grid every bound is exact, from 10 down to 0. A* with the heuristic returns the shortest path in the accent color, 10 hops along the top row and down the right column." width="100%"} A* is only as fast as its heuristic, and many graphs have no natural one (no coordinates, no straight-line distance). ALT (*A\*, Landmarks, Triangle inequality*) builds one from the graph itself: it picks a few *landmark* nodes, measures every node's distance to and from each landmark once, and then bounds the distance between any two nodes using the triangle inequality. The one-time preprocessing pays off when many shortest-path queries are run on the same graph, as in route planning on road networks. The returned function can be passed straight to `astar_path()` or `astar_path_length()` as `heuristic=`. It never overestimates (it is *admissible*) and is *consistent*, so A* still returns shortest paths. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[8]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of landmarks to select (default `8`), capped at the number of nodes. More landmarks give tighter bounds but cost one search each (two on a directed graph) and `k` distances per node of memory. Ignored when `landmarks=` is given. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["farthest"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How landmarks are selected. `"farthest"` (default) picks the first landmark at random and then repeatedly adds the node farthest from its nearest landmark (unreachable nodes count as farthest, so every component gets a landmark). `"random"` picks `k` nodes at random. Ignored when `landmarks=` is given. [landmarks]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int | str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional explicit landmarks, as IDs or labels. Good landmarks are far apart, near the "corners" of the graph; poor ones remain admissible but give looser bounds. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed for the random choices (Python's `random.Random(seed)`). [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. Use the same setting for the A* queries: a heuristic built from different weights may overestimate. Weights must be non-negative. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Callable]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A function `h(u, v)` returning a lower bound on the distance from `u` to `v` (`int` when unweighted). It takes IDs or labels, and its `landmarks` attribute lists the landmark IDs. Nodes added after it was built get the bound `0`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is empty, `k` is less than `1`, `method` is unknown, `landmarks` is empty or names a missing node, or a weight is negative. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The heuristic of Goldberg and Harrelson (2005). For a landmark $\ell$ the triangle inequality gives $d(u, v) \ge d(u, \ell) - d(v, \ell)$ and $d(u, v) \ge d(\ell, v) - d(\ell, u)$; `h(u, v)` is the largest such bound over all landmarks, or `0` if none is finite (for example across components). Each bound is consistent, and so is their maximum (on every edge whose head can reach the target, which are the only edges A* can use on a path to it). Preprocessing runs one Dijkstra search (BFS when unweighted) per landmark, plus one on the reversed graph per landmark when directed, in $O(k (V + E) \log V)$; each call costs $O(k)$. The distances are a snapshot: rebuild the heuristic after changing the graph. Landmark ties go to the smallest ID. This follows NetworkX's proposed `alt_heuristic` (PR #8767, not yet merged). ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 6 x 6 grid, farthest-point selection puts the four landmarks at or next to the corners. The bound between opposite corners is then the exact distance, 10 hops, and A* with the heuristic finds a shortest path: ::: {#c5723088 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(6, 6) ids = sorted(grid.get_node_ids(limit=None)) h = grid.alt_heuristic(k=4, seed=0) h(ids[0], ids[-1]), len(grid.astar_path(ids[0], ids[-1], heuristic=h)) - 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10, 10) ``` ::: :::
